**Observation Log:**

[TEMPORAL] Session Date: 2023/05/27 (Sat) 02:54  
[USER] Strong AI is unusual among theories of the mind in at least two respects: it can be stated clearly, and it admits of a simple and decisive refutation.  
[USER] The refutation is one that any person can try for himself or herself.  
[USER] Consider a language you don't understand. In my case, I do not understand Chinese.  
[USER] To me, Chinese writing looks like so many meaningless squiggles.  
[USER] Suppose I am placed in a room containing baskets full of Chinese symbols.  
[USER] Suppose also that I am given a rule book in English for matching Chinese symbols with other Chinese symbols.  
[USER] The rules identify the symbols entirely by their shapes and do not require that I understand any of them.  
[USER] The rules might say such things as, "Take a squigglesquiggle sign from basket number one and put it next to a squoggle-squoggle sign from basket number two."  
[USER] Imagine that people outside the room who understand Chinese hand in small bunches of symbols and that in response I manipulate the symbols according to the rule book and hand back more small bunches of symbols.  
[USER] Now, the rule book is the "computer program."  
[USER] The people who wrote it are "programmers," and I am the "computer."  
[USER] The baskets full of symbols are the "data base," the small bunches that are handed in to me are "questions," and the bunches I then hand out are "answers."  
[USER] Now suppose that the rule book is written in such a way that my "answers" to the "questions" are indistinguishable from those of a native Chinese speaker.  
[USER] For example, the people outside might hand me some symbols that unknown to me mean, "What's your favorite color?" and I might after going through the rules give back symbols that, also unknown to me, mean, "My favorite is blue, but I also like green a lot."  
[USER] I satisfy the Turing test for understanding Chinese.  
[USER] All the same, I am totally ignorant of Chinese.  
[USER] And there is no way I could come to understand Chinese in the system as described, since there is no way that I can learn the meanings of any of the symbols.  
[USER] Like a computer, I manipulate symbols, but I attach no meaning to the symbols.  
[USER] The point of the thought experiment is this: if I do not understand Chinese solely on the basis of running a computer program for understanding Chinese, then neither does any other digital computer solely on that basis.  
[USER] Digital computers merely manipulate formal symbols according to rules in the program.
